course.title: Data Analytics for Business
course.description: A hands-on first pass at turning raw business data into decisions — the analysis workflow, spreadsheets, clean data, SQL, and honest charts. Topic structure references the Google Career Certificates in Data Analytics; it targets the same Data-Analytics-certificate-style foundations, with all prose and examples original.

questions.prompt: The six phases of the data analysis process are best summarized as…
options: plan, build, test, ship, monitor, close
ask, prepare, process, analyze, share, act
collect, store, secure, delete, audit, report
hypothesize, sample, survey, publish, defend, cite
questions.explanation: The workflow is ask → prepare → process → analyze → share → act — covered in 'The data analysis process'.

questions.prompt: In a spreadsheet, which formula adds the values in cells B2 through B10?
questions.explanation: SUM adds a range; =B2+B10 would only add the two endpoints — see 'Spreadsheets'.

questions.prompt: A pivot table is mainly used to…
options: summarize and group data by categories
questions.explanation: Pivot tables aggregate rows into grouped summaries — see 'Spreadsheets'.

questions.prompt: 'Data integrity' most directly means the data is…
questions.explanation: Integrity is accuracy, completeness, and consistency — see 'Data cleaning & integrity'.

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause filters rows before they are grouped?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows; HAVING filters groups — see 'Querying data with SQL'.

questions.prompt: To compare a single value across a few categories, the clearest chart is usually a…
questions.explanation: Bar charts compare magnitudes cleanly — see 'Visualizing data'.

questions.prompt: A truncated y-axis that starts at 90 instead of 0 tends to…
questions.explanation: Cutting the axis exaggerates differences — see 'Telling a story with data'.

questions.prompt: A dashboard is most useful when it…
options: shows every column in the database
tracks a few key metrics stakeholders act on
replaces the need for any analysis
uses as many colors as possible
questions.explanation: Good dashboards focus on decision-driving metrics — see 'Visualizing data'.

lessons.title: The data analysis process: ask to act
lessons.grammar_note: Six phases, one order: ask → prepare → process → analyze → share → act.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the six phases of the data analysis process and say what each one delivers. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which phase comes right *before* you analyze anything?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Analytics is a workflow, not a single step. The six phases are *ask* (define the business question and who needs it), *prepare* (find and collect the right data), *process* (clean it and check its integrity), *analyze* (calculate, sort, and find patterns), *share* (visualize and communicate the finding), and *act* (make a decision or recommendation). Skipping *ask* is the classic failure: a technically perfect chart that answers the wrong question helps no one.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A store owner asks, 'Which weekday is slowest?' Ask: define 'slow' as revenue. Prepare: pull the sales export. Process: remove test transactions. Analyze: group revenue by weekday. Share: a bar chart shows Tuesday lowest. Act: move the promotion to Tuesday. Each phase fed the next; the recommendation is only as trustworthy as the 'process' step behind it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Place each task in a phase: (1) interviewing the marketing lead about their goal, (2) deleting rows with impossible negative ages, (3) building the slide that reveals the trend, (4) writing 'we recommend pausing Product B'. Answers: (1) ask, (2) process, (3) share, (4) act.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'analyze' as the whole job — without *ask* it is aimless, without *share* no one uses it. Mistake: thinking the phases never loop (a weak analysis often sends you back to prepare). Exit: (a) Which phase defines the business question? (b) Which phase includes cleaning? Answers: ask; process.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets: formulas and pivot tables
lessons.grammar_note: A formula starts with '='; a function like SUM takes a range such as B2:B10.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write core spreadsheet formulas and build a pivot table to summarize data. Warm-up: what single character must every spreadsheet formula begin with?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A spreadsheet formula begins with `=` and often calls a *function* over a *range*. The everyday toolkit: `SUM` and `AVERAGE` aggregate a range; `COUNTIF` counts rows matching a condition; `IF` returns one of two values on a test; `VLOOKUP` pulls a matching value from another table. A *pivot table* takes a long table of rows and collapses it into grouped totals — the point-and-click version of SQL's GROUP BY — letting you see, say, revenue per region without writing a formula per region.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Given sales in B2:B10 and regions in A2:A10:
```
=SUM(B2:B10)              → 4820   (total sales)
=AVERAGE(B2:B10)          → 535.6  (mean per order)
=COUNTIF(A2:A10,"West")   → 3      (orders from West)
=IF(B2>500,"big","small") → "big"  (flags large orders)
=VLOOKUP("West",D2:E5,2,FALSE) → 12   (West's target from a lookup table)
```
A pivot table on the same data with region as rows and SUM of sales as values would output one line per region: East 1600, North 1420, West 1800.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Write a formula for each: (1) the largest order in B2:B10, (2) how many orders exceed 500 in B2:B10, (3) the average of C2:C20. Answers: (1) `=MAX(B2:B10)`, (2) `=COUNTIF(B2:B10,">500")`, (3) `=AVERAGE(C2:C20)`.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the leading `=`, so the cell shows text instead of computing. Mistake: giving VLOOKUP the wrong column index or omitting `FALSE` for an exact match. Exit: (a) Which function counts rows meeting a condition? (b) A pivot table is the spreadsheet cousin of which SQL clause? Answers: COUNTIF; GROUP BY.

lessons.title: Data cleaning and integrity
lessons.grammar_note: Integrity = accurate + complete + consistent. Clean before you analyze, never after.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Spot common data-quality problems and explain why cleaning must come before analysis. Warm-up: name one thing that makes a dataset untrustworthy.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Data integrity* means the data is accurate, complete, and consistent across its life. Real exports rarely arrive that way: they carry *duplicate* rows, *missing* values, inconsistent formats ('NY' vs 'New York'), leading/trailing spaces, and impossible outliers (an age of 210). *Cleaning* is the disciplined removal or repair of these issues. It matters because every later step multiplies the error — 'garbage in, garbage out'. A duplicated order inflates revenue; a stray text value breaks an AVERAGE.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A 1,000-row customer export: 14 exact duplicate rows, 30 blank emails, and states typed as both 'CA' and 'California'. Cleaning: remove the 14 duplicates (now 986 rows), decide blanks are 'unknown' rather than 0, and standardize every state to the two-letter code. In a spreadsheet you might flag duplicates with `=COUNTIF($A$2:$A$1000,A2)>1` — any TRUE is a repeat to inspect. Only now is a revenue total meaningful.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each issue: (1) the same invoice appears twice, (2) a price cell is empty, (3) dates stored as both 2026-07-01 and 07/01/2026, (4) a customer age of -5. Answers: (1) duplicate, (2) missing value, (3) inconsistent format, (4) invalid/outlier value.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: filling missing numbers with 0, which silently drags averages down — 'unknown' is not zero. Mistake: cleaning a copy but analyzing the original. Exit: (a) Name the three parts of data integrity. (b) Why clean before analyzing? Answers: accurate, complete, consistent; because errors compound in every later step.

questions.prompt: Which phase of the process directly precedes 'analyze'?
questions.explanation: Order is ask, prepare, process, analyze, share, act.

questions.prompt: `=COUNTIF(A2:A100,"West")` returns…
options: the number of rows equal to 'West'
questions.explanation: COUNTIF counts rows matching the condition.

questions.prompt: A pivot table most resembles which SQL clause?
questions.explanation: Both aggregate rows into grouped summaries.

questions.prompt: Two rows for the same invoice number is an example of…
questions.explanation: The record is repeated.

questions.prompt: Replacing missing prices with 0 is risky because it…
questions.explanation: 0 is treated as a real low value, biasing means.

questions.prompt: Data integrity is defined as accurate, complete, and…
questions.explanation: Accurate + complete + consistent.

lessons.title: Querying data with SQL basics
lessons.grammar_note: Clause order that matters: SELECT … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … ORDER BY. WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and write a basic SQL query that filters, groups, and sorts data. Warm-up: which clause chooses *which columns* you get back?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: SQL asks a database questions. A query names the columns in `SELECT`, the table in `FROM`, a row filter in `WHERE`, a grouping in `GROUP BY`, aggregate math like `SUM` or `COUNT`, and a sort in `ORDER BY`. The mental order is: take the table, keep rows that pass WHERE, collapse them into groups, compute an aggregate per group, then sort. `WHERE` filters *before* grouping; `HAVING` filters the groups *after*.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
From an `orders` table with columns region, amount, status:
```
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY total_sales DESC;
```
This keeps only paid orders, adds up `amount` per region, and lists regions highest first — e.g. West 1800, East 1600, North 1420. To keep only strong regions, add `HAVING SUM(amount) > 1500` before ORDER BY, which would drop North.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer for the query above: (1) which clause removes unpaid orders? (2) which clause makes West appear first? (3) write a query counting orders per status. Answers: (1) `WHERE status = 'paid'`; (2) `ORDER BY total_sales DESC`; (3) `SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY status;`.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using `WHERE` to filter an aggregate (e.g. `WHERE SUM(amount) > 1500`) — that must be `HAVING`. Mistake: selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated. Exit: (a) Which clause filters groups after aggregation? (b) Which sorts the result? Answers: HAVING; ORDER BY.

lessons.title: Visualizing data and telling an honest story
lessons.grammar_note: Match the chart to the job: bars compare, lines show change over time, pies show parts of one whole.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose an appropriate chart, design a focused dashboard, and spot a misleading one. Warm-up: which chart type best shows a value changing month by month?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A visualization's job is to make the finding obvious. Rules of thumb: *bar charts* compare categories, *line charts* show change over time, *pie charts* show parts of a single whole (and only when there are a few slices). A *dashboard* collects a few key metrics that stakeholders check regularly — focused, not exhaustive. Honesty is part of the craft: a *truncated y-axis* (starting above zero) exaggerates small gaps, a dual axis can imply a fake correlation, and a pie with fifteen slices hides the story. The same data can mislead or clarify depending on these choices.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Revenue rose from 102 to 108 over six months (+5.9%). On a y-axis starting at 100, the bar for month six looks roughly four times taller than month one — visually screaming 'huge growth'. Redraw the axis from 0 and the bars are nearly level: modest, honest growth. Same numbers, opposite impression. For a dashboard, three tiles — total revenue, revenue trend line, and top-region bar — beat a wall of twenty charts.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Pick the chart or verdict: (1) sales for Jan–Dec, (2) market share of 3 competitors, (3) revenue by 5 regions, (4) a chart whose y-axis starts at 95 to show '2% growth'. Answers: (1) line chart, (2) pie chart, (3) bar chart, (4) misleading — the truncated axis exaggerates the change.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using a pie chart for many categories or for values that aren't parts of one whole. Mistake: assuming a scary-looking chart is wrong on purpose — often it's a careless default axis. Exit: (a) Which chart shows change over time? (b) What does starting a y-axis above zero do to differences? Answers: line chart; it exaggerates them.

questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

questions.explanation: GROUP BY yields one aggregated row per region.

questions.prompt: The clearest chart for revenue across twelve months is a…
questions.explanation: Line charts show change over time.

questions.explanation: Focus on decision-driving metrics.

questions.explanation: A truncated axis inflates visual gaps.

questions.prompt: To keep only groups whose total exceeds 1500, you add…
questions.explanation: HAVING filters aggregated groups.

lessons.title: Applied project: analyze a business dataset and present findings

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Take a small business dataset you can access or invent realistically — for example a month of orders with columns date, region, product, and amount. Walk it through the full process and present a single, defensible finding to a stakeholder. You are not graded on tools; you are graded on rigor and clarity.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Ask: write the one business question ('Which region should we grow?'). 2) Process: list two data-quality checks you ran (e.g. removed duplicates, standardized region names). 3) Analyze: state the calculation — describe the pivot table or the SQL, e.g. `SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY 2 DESC;`. 4) Share: describe the one chart you'd show and why that chart type. 5) Act: give a one-sentence recommendation the stakeholder can act on.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The question is specific and tied to a decision. ✔ You named real cleaning steps, not just 'I cleaned it'. ✔ Your calculation would actually answer the question (right GROUP BY / right aggregate). ✔ The chart matches the job (bar to compare, line for time). ✔ The recommendation follows from the finding and uses an honest axis. If all five hold, you've completed one full loop of the data analysis process.
